deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 13-15): Grothendieck studies functionals on L^∞ of a finite measure space K that are invariant under equimeasurable rearrangement. He calls them 'fonctions de Weyl' and 'fonctions de Pólya', after Hardy-Littlewood-Pólya majorization. The aim is to reduce such a functional P on L^∞(K) to a functional P* of the decreasing rearrangement φ_f on ]0,|K|] or R^+. This is a general theory of rearrangement-invariant convex functionals that contains the L^p and Orlicz/Lorentz-type examples of the previous page.

Top lines. A convex set already known to be closed for some weak topology is shown to be closed for σ(L^∞(K), L^1(K)). The passage (partly struck) appears to go from closedness for the weak topology σ(L^∞, (L^∞)') to weak* closedness, with a parenthetical reason concerning L^∞(K) that is hard to read.

Main argument. Let P: L^∞(K) → R satisfy three properties:
- P_1: rearrangement invariance, P(f) = P(g) whenever f and g are equimeasurable.
- P_2: convexity.
- P'_3: weak* lower semicontinuity.

The epigraph A_P = {(λ,f) ∈ R × L^∞ : λ ≥ P(f)} is convex by P_2 and σ(L^∞,L^1)-closed by P'_3. By Hahn-Banach in the dual pair (L^∞, L^1), A_P is the intersection of the closed half-spaces containing it. Since P is finite, these can be taken non-vertical: λ ≥ L_i(f) + a_i with L_i ∈ L^1(K) and a_i ∈ R. Hence P(f) = sup_i (L_i(f) + a_i), the Fenchel-Moreau biconjugate representation.

By P_1, P(f) = P(g) ≥ L_i(g) + a_i for every g equimeasurable with f. 'Prop. 2' then gives sup_{g~f} ∫ L_i g = ∫ φ_{L_i} φ_f, where φ denotes the decreasing rearrangement. This is the Hardy-Littlewood inequality together with its attainment (or approximation) on a non-atomic space. Therefore P(f) ≥ a_i + ∫ φ_i φ_f. Conversely the Hardy-Littlewood inequality gives L_i(f) ≤ ∫ φ_i φ_f, so equality holds.

Result, formula (1): P(f) = sup_{i∈I} (a_i + ∫_0^{|K|} φ_i φ_f), with φ_i decreasing functions in L^1(]0,|K|]). The next page notes the converse (any such formula defines a 'Pólya function'). It then specializes: P is increasing iff the φ_i are positive. It rewrites the result as P(f) = P*(φ_f), a convex functional on decreasing functions on R^+.

In modern terms: every proper, convex, weak*-lsc, law-invariant functional on L^∞ of an atomless finite measure space is a supremum of affine functionals built from 'spectral' (quantile-weighted) integrals ∫ φ_i(t) f*(t) dt. This is exactly the Kusuoka-type representation of law-invariant convex functionals.
errors: Hahn-Banach yields closed half-spaces μλ ≥ L(f)+a with possibly μ = 0 (vertical). Asserting they are 'forcément' of the form λ ≥ L_i(f)+a_i needs P finite (proper) everywhere, or a short extra argument. It is a standard gap, easily filled.

Prop. 2 (sup over g equimeasurable with f of ∫ L g = ∫ φ_L φ_f) needs K non-atomic, or at least is only correct as a supremum, not a maximum, in general. On spaces with atoms the representation must be modified. The page does not state the hypothesis (it may be in the earlier setup).
For signed f, φ_f must be the decreasing rearrangement of f itself, not of |f|, for the formula to be correct. The notation leaves this implicit.

The top-of-page passage deducing σ(L^∞,L^1)-closedness from closedness in a weaker sense is not justified as legible. In general, norm-closed or σ(L^∞,(L^∞)')-closed convex sets need not be weak* closed. That implication is true only using rearrangement invariance on an atomless space (later 'automatic Fatou property'). It is unclear whether Grothendieck invokes this.

ideas.what: Representation of a convex, weak*-lsc, rearrangement-invariant functional on L^∞(K) as sup_i (a_i + ∫ φ_i φ_f), with φ_i decreasing and integrable and φ_f the decreasing rearrangement of f
ideas.modern_name: Kusuoka-type representation of law-invariant convex functionals / spectral (distortion) representation; dual representation of rearrangement-invariant convex functions
ideas.usually_credited_to: For r.i. norms: Lorentz (1950s), Luxemburg (1955/1967). For law-invariant coherent risk measures: Kusuoka (2001). For law-invariant convex risk measures: Frittelli-Rosazza Gianin (2005), Dana (2005), Jouini-Schachermayer-Touzi (2006).
ideas.where_published: Not in his published functional analysis work as far as I know; unsure whether anything similar appears in the 1954 São Paulo course notes.

ideas.what: Use of the epigraph and Hahn-Banach to write a convex weak*-lsc function as a sup of continuous affine functions
Prop. 2: sup over g equimeasurable with f of ∫ L g = ∫ L* f*
ideas.modern_name: Hardy-Littlewood rearrangement inequality and its sharpness on non-atomic spaces

ideas.what: Reduction P(f) = P*(φ_f) to a convex functional on decreasing functions on R^+ (next page)
ideas.modern_name: Rearrangement-invariant functionals as functionals of the quantile function / Luxemburg representation theorem

missed.claim: In 1953 Grothendieck proved what is essentially the Kusuoka / Frittelli-Rosazza Gianin representation of law-invariant convex lsc functionals on L^∞ as suprema of affine spectral functionals a_i + ∫ φ_i f*. It is a cornerstone of modern risk-measure theory (2001-2006). He also had the monotone (positive φ_i) and sublinear variants on the next page. This prefigures that literature by roughly 50 years and is not cited there.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority and a missed bridge between Grothendieck's r.i. function-space work and mathematical finance (law-invariant risk measures, distortion/spectral risk measures). His general 'fonctions de Pólya/Weyl' framework also covers non-monotone and non-positively-homogeneous cases.

missed.claim: The opening lines seem to address when closedness of a rearrangement-invariant convex set implies weak* (σ(L^∞,L^1)) closedness. If Grothendieck proved norm-closed r.i. convex ⇒ weak* closed, this is the 'automatic Fatou property' of Jouini-Schachermayer-Touzi (2006). The page is too fragmentary to confirm.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: If confirmed from the previous pages, it would be an early instance of a result considered non-trivial in 2006.

deep.surprise_reason: The representation theorem is clean and correct and anticipates the Kusuoka-type representations of law-invariant convex functionals (2001-2005). The r.i.-norm case was, however, close to known material of Lorentz and Luxemburg in the 1950s, and the proof uses standard tools (Hahn-Banach plus Hardy-Littlewood). The connection to the later finance literature is real but the mathematics itself would not shock an analyst.
transcription_corrections: The struck-out 'P(f) = Sup' line before the formula is visibly struck; the marginal text at left is a long vertical note (roughly 'Commencer par ... a ...' and 'Vous faites ... (illisible)') bracketing the whole argument, not just a single word.
Top line probably reads '...topologie faible) dans l'espace conjugué de L^1(K), d'où ...', with the second line struck through entirely.
Third line reads 'pour σ(L^∞(K)... L^∞(K)'), donc (... dans L^∞(K))' — the dual in the first σ is likely (L^∞)' rather than L^∞; the parenthetical is illegible, not clearly 'étant fermé'.
In formula (1) the superscript over the integral sign is a struck/overwritten '(K)' (domain of integration), and the boxed formula is P(f) = Sup_{i∈I} a_i + ∫ φ_i φ_f.
